newsitem.title: USA: Digital Equipment meeting seen pressuring CEO Palmer.
newsitem.headline: Digital Equipment meeting seen pressuring CEO Palmer.

text.p: The institutional shareholders of Digital Equipment Corp. will have plenty to grumble about when they meet this week in New York.

Despite management shake-ups, restructurings and massive layoffs, the nation's fourth-largest computer company has lost billions of dollars over the past few years and is on the verge of reporting disappointing results for another year.

Since Robert Palmer was named chief executive in October 1992, Digital's shares have fallen 15 percent to around $36 a share while the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks has nearly doubled in value.
That has provoked a small New York investment firm with a history of corporate activism to invite institutional shareholders to gather and discuss Digital's prospects.
Herbert Denton, president of Providence Capital Inc., said he expected institutions representing more than 30 percent of Digital's shares to attend the meeting on Wednesday.
A Digital spokesman said the company's executives had no plans to show up, but that they were in regular contact with shareholders and also were not pleased with performance.

"We have a very strong investor relations program. We talk to our investors regularly," spokesman Dan Kaferle said. "We're not satisfied with our performance. We know we can do better and we're going to do better."

Terry Shannon, editor of the newsletter "Shannon Knows DEC", has been invited to speak at the meeting and plans to tell the shareholders that while Digital's technology has been superior, its marketing has been a disaster.
"I've said for years that products and technology are not the problem, it's the marketing," he said. "Digital's really got to do something with respect to getting the word out."
Providence Capital's Denton holds a small amount of Digital stock, and major institutions such as mutual fund companies and investment management firms declined to say if they would attend.
Whether Denton proves to be a leader of frustrated shareholders or just a footnote in Digital's troubled history, the meeting is expected to put additional pressure on Palmer, analysts said.

"I think even without the meeting, there's been probably a reasonable amount of pressure to perform," said Laura Conigliaro at Goldman Sachs & Co. "At some point, I think it becomes clear that patience wears thin."

At November's annual meeting, Palmer said he expected earnings of more than $1 a share for the fiscal year ending this month but actually hoped to top the $2.23 a share, or $380 million, reported in fiscal 1996 before restructuring charges. Instead, Wall Street analysts surveyed by First Call are now estimating earnings of about 65 cents a share.
After a restructuring charge of $492 million, Digitial reported a net loss of $111 million, 97 cents a share, for fiscal 1996.
Palmer also faces other hurdles.

Sure to be topics of discussion at the meeting are Compaq Computer Corp.'s reported takeover bid, Digital's patent lawsuit against Intel Corp., and another management shakeup scheduled to go into effect on July 1.

According to the Wall Street Journal, Digital turned down Compaq's 1995 offer of about $60 a share because of fears it would lose its independence. Digital and Compaq have declined to comment on the report.

Intel, after Digital filed a patent lawsuit, has threatened to cut off key supplies of its Pentium chips at the end of the third quarter. Should Intel do so, it probably would hurt Digital's sales of Pentium-based computers, which accounted for more than $2 billion in revenue last year.
Meanwhile, sales of Digital's alternative to the Pentium, the faster Alpha chip, have been lackluster and are expected to slow in the fourth quarter, analysts said.
"They've had a year of disappointment on Alpha," said Gary Helmig at Soundview Financial Group. "The guidance is they would expect Alpha to be down from the fourth quarter of last year."
